newsitem.title: USA: Cholesterol-lowering drug may cut stroke risk.
newsitem.headline: Cholesterol-lowering drug may cut stroke risk.

text.p: A class of cholesterol-cutting drugs have proven to protect against stroke and potentially fatal cardiovascular disease, researchers said on Tuesday.

In an analysis of 16 previous trials encompassing 29,000 subjects, researchers at Vanderbilt University School of Medicine found statin drugs reduced the risk of stroke by 29 percent and lowered total mortality rates by 22 percent.

Statin drugs also produced larger reductions in cholesterol than previously available lipid-lowering drugs, cutting blood cholesterol levels by an average of 22 percent, the report in the Journal of the American Medical Association said.

"This overview of all published trials of statin drugs demonstrates their effectiveness in reducing cholesterol and provides clear evidence of benefits on stroke and mortality," study author Patricia Hebert wrote.
There was no significant evidence that lowering cholesterol levels with the drugs led to any increase in the incidence of cancer or other non-heart-related deaths.
While previous research has shown that lowering cholesterol decreases the risk of coronary heart disease, its effect on the risk of stroke and total mortality had been unclear.

Charles Hennekens of Harvard Medical School and a senior author of the study suggested wider use of these drugs. "However, it is also important to note that not everyone with elevated cholesterol should be treated with statin drugs."
For most people, a healthy diet and lifestyle is the best defence against heart disease, the authors said.
